date_label: Met on a Washington horsecar one stormy winter evening, 1865 by the scholarship and 1866 by Doyle's own reckoning; closest through the Washington years to about 1873, renewed in the mid-1880s when Doyle moved to Philadelphia, and running until Whitman's death on 26 March 1892
summary: Peter Doyle was twenty-one and conducting a Pennsylvania Avenue horsecar on a stormy night when Walt Whitman, forty-five, boarded as its only passenger with a blanket round his shoulders. By Doyle's account they understood one another before either had spoken much. They spent the Washington years riding the streetcars, eating fruit at Center Market and walking the Potomac by moonlight - Whitman reciting Shakespeare's sonnets, Doyle telling limericks - and Whitman was taken into Doyle's family. Whitman's stroke in 1873 and his move to Camden put a river and a state between them and the intensity cooled; Harry Stafford filled some of the gap in New Jersey. Doyle moved to Philadelphia in the mid-1880s and visited weekly until the nurses of Whitman's last years crowded him out. He came to the funeral. In 1897 he let Bucke print Whitman's letters to him, which is the only reason the relationship is documented at all; his own letters to Whitman largely are not.

sources.quote: You ask where I first met him? It is a curious story. We felt to each other at once. I was a conductor. The night was very stormy,—he had been over to see Burroughs before he came down to take the car—the storm was awful. Walt had his blanket—it was thrown round his shoulders—he seemed like an old sea-captain. He was the only passenger, it was a lonely night, so I thought I would go in and talk with him. Something in me made me do it and something in him drew me that way. He used to say there was something in me had the same effect on him. Anyway, I went into the car. We were familiar at once—I put my hand on his knee—we understood. He did not get out at the end of the trip—in fact went all the way back with me. I think the year of this was 1866. From that time on we were the biggest sort of friends.
sources.context: Doyle, interviewed by Richard Maurice Bucke and printed verbatim in Bucke's introduction under its own running head, 'INTERVIEW WITH PETER DOYLE'. This is the only substantial first-person account Doyle left of the relationship, and the source every later account of the meeting quotes. Note his own hedge on the year: the scholarship dates the meeting to 1865, Doyle says he thinks it was 1866. Henry James, reviewing the book in 1898, called this interview the most charming passage in the volume.
sources.supports: The meeting, in the other participant's own words - and the class, since it puts Doyle's voice beside Whitman's rather than leaving the edge resting on Whitman alone.

sources.quote: New York, Friday, 25 Sept., 1868. Dear Boy. I received your second letter yesterday—it is a real comfort to me to get such letters from you, dear friend. Every word does me good. … I put down off hand and write all about myself and my doings, etc., because I suppose that will be really what my dear comrade wants most to hear while we are separated.
sources.context: The first letter Bucke prints, opening the section headed 'LETTERS OF 1868'. The salutation is the volume's standard: Whitman writes to Doyle as 'Dear Boy', 'Dear Boy and Comrade' and 'Dear Pete' across the run. The elision drops two sentences about a newspaper and the timing of the post. Small capitals in the printed salutation normalised.
sources.supports: Whitman's own register toward Doyle at the start of the correspondence - 'dear friend', 'my dear comrade' - and the fact of a sustained private correspondence.

sources.quote: The romantic friendship that Walt Whitman shared with Peter Doyle embodied the "love of comrades" celebrated in Whitman's "Calamus" poems. Their thirty-year friendship (1865–1892) left a legacy of loving letters from the older man to his younger companion which are invaluable reference points for the student seeking to understand Whitman's emotional and sexual nature.
sources.context: The opening of Martin G. Murray's reference entry on Doyle, the standard short account and by the author of the fullest published biography of him. Recorded as the second-hand layer: it names the relationship 'romantic friendship' and points the reader at the letters for the sexual question without answering it. Murray also supplies the detail that Doyle was twenty-one and Whitman forty-five at the meeting, and that Doyle is buried in Congressional Cemetery.
sources.supports: The scholarly characterisation of the relationship, and its span - corroboration, not the basis of the class.

null_findings.finding: ASYMMETRY WORTH KNOWING BEFORE ANYONE HUNTS FOR MORE. The volume is Whitman's letters TO Doyle plus Bucke's interview OF Doyle; **Doyle's own letters to Whitman are not in it**. Doyle kept Whitman's and gave them to Bucke in 1880; the reverse run largely does not survive, so apart from the interview this relationship is documented in one direction, like hall--souline. A few Doyle-to-Whitman letters are held elsewhere and are transcribed on the Whitman Archive (e.g. item nyp.00304, Doyle to Whitman, 5-6 October 1868) - not consulted here, and the obvious next step if this edge is ever deepened.
